Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "i am revising the order form for maple & rye bakery, and i need the wording and field sequence to be easier for customers and staff to follow. the form is used for cakes, pastry boxes, bread orders, and a small number of catered trays. it should still feel like one form, not four separate forms, because some customers order more than one kind of item at the same time. please help make the request clear without changing what the form asks people to do. the bakery takes orders online and at the counter, but staff enter counter orders into the same system before the end of the day.

at the top, customers should choose pickup or delivery, then give their name, phone number, and email address. the phone number is the best way to contact them if a detail is missing, but we still need the email for the written confirmation. the delivery option is available only within the bakery's local delivery area, which is printed on a separate map linked beside the choice. if a customer selects delivery and enters an address outside that area, the form should not accept the delivery selection; it should ask the customer to choose pickup instead. don't hide the pickup choice in that situation. a delivery address field should appear only after delivery is chosen, while pickup customers should not have to fill in an address.

we need the requested date and a time window on every order. for pickup, the choices are 9:00–11:00 a.m., 11:00 a.m.–1:00 p.m., and 1:00–3:00 p.m. for delivery, the choices are 10:00 a.m.–noon and noon–2:00 p.m. the time choices should change with the service choice so someone does not see a pickup window on a delivery order. if a customer selects pickup and submits the form by 3 p.m. at least two business days before the requested date, staff should hold the selected pickup window. if either the 3 p.m. cutoff or the two-business-day lead time is missed, staff should not promise that window and should offer the next available pickup window instead. the same cutoff rule is not a promise that an order is accepted; the bakery still has to check the items and confirm the order.

for delivery, the form should show a note that deliveries are scheduled in the two listed windows, not at an exact minute. a customer can enter a preferred delivery window, but that preference is subject to route capacity. if the preferred window is full, staff should offer the other listed window before they confirm. if neither window can be used on that date, staff should contact the customer to ask whether another date works; do not move the date without asking. delivery charges are calculated from the address and appear in the order total before payment. pickup has no delivery charge. customers can pay by card online or select pay at pickup for pickup orders; pay at pickup should not appear for delivery orders.

next, the form needs an item section that lets a customer add several lines to one order. for each line, ask for the product name, quantity, and any size or serving choice that applies. cake sizes are 6-inch, 8-inch, and 10-inch; the serving estimates beside them are 8, 12, and 20 portions. pastry boxes come in 6-piece and 12-piece sizes, while bread is ordered by loaf. these choices should only be displayed for the relevant product, rather than shown together as if a loaf had a cake size. catered trays are listed in small and large sizes, and staff will confirm the serving estimate for those after they review the order.

cake customers should have a separate space for flavor, filling, and decoration notes. the standard cake flavors are vanilla, chocolate, and lemon, and the fillings are raspberry, chocolate ganache, and vanilla cream. decoration notes are requests, not a guarantee that every design can be made. the form should say, “Please describe the colors or theme you have in mind; we will confirm what we can provide.” if a customer asks for writing on a cake, include a text field with a 30-character limit. the limit applies to the writing only, not to the decoration notes. pastry box customers can list up to three pastry types in the notes field, but the form should not imply that every type is available every day.

we also need a clearly worded allergy field. customers can identify an allergy or enter “none,” and the form must not treat a blank allergy field as the same as “none.” a note beside it should say that the bakery handles wheat, eggs, milk, peanuts, and tree nuts in the same kitchen. if a customer reports an allergy, the form should flag the order for staff review before confirmation. that flag does not itself mean the bakery can safely prepare the order, and the confirmation message should not promise an allergy-free product. customers should be able to add other dietary notes, but those notes should stay separate from the allergy response.

1. order review and confirmation
before payment, show the customer a review with service type, date, window, address when applicable, each item and quantity, notes, charges, and total. if a customer uses pay at pickup, show the amount due without asking for card details. the submit button should say “Send order request,” since sending the form does not mean the bakery has accepted the order. after submission, show, “Your request has been received. We will contact you after reviewing availability and details.” the emailed copy should include the requested date and all entered notes, so the customer and staff can check the same information.

staff need the submitted order to show when it arrived, whether the customer chose pickup or delivery, and whether an allergy response was entered. orders arriving by counter entry should retain the time staff entered them, not the time the customer first came into the shop. this matters for the two-business-day pickup check: staff use the system entry time to decide whether the cutoff has been met. the form should not automatically label an order late or reject it based only on the requested date, because staff may need to discuss a different date or window with the customer. keep the originally requested date visible even if the customer later agrees to a change.

customers sometimes need to correct an order after sending it. the confirmation email should tell them to call the bakery rather than submit a second form, and the staff record should keep the initial request visible alongside any change agreed to by phone. if an order has not yet been confirmed, staff can update its details after speaking with the customer; if it has been confirmed, staff should first check whether the requested change is still possible. the form itself should not claim that an edit has been made just because someone called. this distinction is important when an item, delivery address, or requested window changes, since the kitchen and delivery list use the confirmed details.

please keep the page readable on a phone, with short labels and the explanation placed beside the relevant field. the separate delivery-area map should remain linked near the service choice, and the allergy note should be visible before a customer submits. we do not need a promotional message or a long description of the bakery on this form. the goal is for customers to enter a complete request, understand what is only a preference, and know that staff will review the order before it is confirmed. the final wording should work for online customers and for staff entering a counter order, including when the customer needs to be contacted about a date, window, or allergy response.", "output": "I am revising the order form for Maple & Rye Bakery and need the wording and field sequence to be easier for customers and staff to follow. The form is used for cakes, pastry boxes, bread orders, and a small number of catered trays. It should still feel like one form, not four separate forms, because some customers order more than one kind of item at the same time. Please make the request clear without changing what the form asks people to do. The bakery takes orders online and at the counter, but staff enter counter orders into the same system before the end of the day.

At the top, customers should choose pickup or delivery, then provide their name, phone number, and email address. The phone number is the best way to contact them if a detail is missing, but the email is still needed for the written confirmation. Delivery is available only within the bakery’s local delivery area, which is shown on a separate map linked beside the choice. If a customer selects delivery and enters an address outside that area, the form should not accept the delivery selection. Instead, it should ask the customer to choose pickup. Do not hide the pickup choice in that situation. The delivery address field should appear only after delivery is selected, and pickup customers should not have to enter an address.

We need the requested date and a time window for every order. For pickup, the choices are 9:00–11:00 a.m., 11:00 a.m.–1:00 p.m., and 1:00–3:00 p.m. For delivery, the choices are 10:00 a.m.–noon and noon–2:00 p.m. The time choices should change with the service choice so customers do not see a pickup window on a delivery order. If a customer selects pickup and submits the form by 3 p.m. at least two business days before the requested date, staff should hold the selected pickup window. If either the 3 p.m. cutoff or the two-business-day lead time is missed, staff should not promise that window and should offer the next available pickup window instead. Meeting the cutoff does not guarantee that an order will be accepted; the bakery still has to check the items and confirm the order.

For delivery, the form should note that deliveries are scheduled in the two listed windows, not at an exact minute. Customers can enter a preferred delivery window, but that preference is subject to route capacity. If the preferred window is full, staff should offer the other listed window before confirming. If neither window is available on that date, staff should contact the customer to ask whether another date works. Do not change the date without asking. Delivery charges are calculated from the address and appear in the order total before payment. Pickup has no delivery charge. Customers can pay by card online or select pay at pickup for pickup orders. The pay-at-pickup option should not appear for delivery orders.

Next, the form needs an item section that lets customers add several lines to one order. For each line, ask for the product name, quantity, and any applicable size or serving choice. Cake sizes are 6-inch, 8-inch, and 10-inch, with serving estimates of 8, 12, and 20 portions. Pastry boxes come in 6-piece and 12-piece sizes, while bread is ordered by the loaf. Show these choices only for the relevant product, rather than together as if a loaf had a cake size. Catered trays are listed in small and large sizes, and staff will confirm their serving estimates after reviewing the order.

Cake customers should have separate spaces for flavor, filling, and decoration notes. The standard cake flavors are vanilla, chocolate, and lemon; fillings are raspberry, chocolate ganache, and vanilla cream. Decoration notes are requests, not a guarantee that every design can be made. The form should say, “Please describe the colors or theme you have in mind; we will confirm what we can provide.” If a customer asks for writing on a cake, include a text field with a 30-character limit. The limit applies to the writing only, not the decoration notes. Pastry box customers can list up to three pastry types in the notes field, but the form should not imply that every type is available every day.

We also need a clearly worded allergy field. Customers can identify an allergy or enter “none,” and the form must not treat a blank allergy field as the same as “none.” A note beside it should say that the bakery handles wheat, eggs, milk, peanuts, and tree nuts in the same kitchen. If a customer reports an allergy, the form should flag the order for staff review before confirmation. That flag does not mean the bakery can safely prepare the order, and the confirmation message should not promise an allergy-free product. Customers should be able to add other dietary notes, but those notes should remain separate from the allergy response.

1. Order review and confirmation

Before payment, show the customer a review with the service type, date, window, address when applicable, each item and quantity, notes, charges, and total. If a customer uses pay at pickup, show the amount due without asking for card details. The submit button should say “Send order request,” since sending the form does not mean the bakery has accepted the order. After submission, show, “Your request has been received. We will contact you after reviewing availability and details.” The emailed copy should include the requested date and all entered notes, so the customer and staff can check the same information.

Staff need to see when the order arrived, whether the customer chose pickup or delivery, and whether an allergy response was entered. Orders entered by staff from the counter should retain the time they were entered into the system, not the time the customer first came into the shop. This matters for the two-business-day pickup check: staff use the system entry time to decide whether the cutoff has been met. The form should not automatically label an order late or reject it based only on the requested date, because staff may need to discuss a different date or window with the customer. Keep the originally requested date visible even if the customer later agrees to a change.

Customers sometimes need to correct an order after sending it. The confirmation email should tell them to call the bakery rather than submit a second form, and the staff record should keep the initial request visible alongside any change agreed to by phone. If an order has not yet been confirmed, staff can update its details after speaking with the customer. If it has been confirmed, staff should first check whether the requested change is still possible. The form itself should not claim that an edit has been made just because someone called. This distinction matters when an item, delivery address, or requested window changes, since the kitchen and delivery list use the confirmed details.

Please keep the page readable on a phone, with short labels and explanations beside the relevant fields. The separate delivery-area map should remain linked near the service choice, and the allergy note should be visible before a customer submits the form. We do not need a promotional message or a long description of the bakery on this form. The goal is for customers to enter a complete request, understand what is only a preference, and know that staff will review the order before it is confirmed. The final wording should work for online customers and for staff entering a counter order, including when a customer needs to be contacted about a date, window, or allergy response."}]
